name: Roll out and roll back a Deployment
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment. Drill EVERY way to change a Deployment that already exists — WITHOUT deleting it: scale, rolling image update, rollback, set resources, inject config, change strategy, targeted JSON patch, and rollout restart. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Scale in place
questions.teach:
`kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=N` changes only `.spec.replicas` — it doesn't touch the pod template, so no rollout happens. Never delete+recreate just to change replica count.

**Gotcha:** an **HPA** targeting the Deployment overrides a manual `scale` within seconds.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `frontend` in `deploy-learn` exists with 2 replicas. Scale it **in place** to **4**.

Target: `frontend` has 4 ready replicas (and you did not delete it).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend

verification.description: frontend scaled to 4 ready replicas (in place)

questions.eli5:
A **Deployment** is like a thermostat for pods: you set a target number of copies (replicas) and Kubernetes keeps exactly that many running. If one dies, it makes another; if there are too many, it removes some.

**Scaling** is just turning that dial. `kubectl scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4` says "I want 4 copies now." Kubernetes spins up 2 more (from 2 to 4) and that's it. You never tear down the Deployment — you just change one number.

The key insight: scaling touches **only** the replica count. It does **not** touch the pod template (the image, env, resources), so **no rollout happens** — the existing pods keep running untouched, and new identical ones just join them.

**Watch out for:**

- **Never delete-and-recreate just to change the count.** Scaling is the right, in-place way.
- **Scaling does not trigger a rollout** — only template changes do. The current pods are undisturbed; new ones are added (or extra ones removed).
- **An HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) will override you.** If something is autoscaling `frontend`, your manual `--replicas=4` gets reset within seconds to whatever the HPA wants. Check with `kubectl get hpa` first.
- **Scaling to 0** is legal and stops all pods without deleting the Deployment — handy for pausing a workload.
- Scaling **up** means new pods must still *fit* (resources) and *schedule* — if the cluster is full, the extras sit `Pending`.
questions.deepDive:
## Scale a Deployment in place — full rundown

### Mental model
A Deployment's `.spec.replicas` is the **desired count**. The Deployment controls a ReplicaSet, which reconciles actual pods toward that number. `kubectl scale` edits only that one field — the **pod template is untouched**, so there is **no rollout**; the controller merely adds or removes pods.

### The command
```bash
kubectl scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4
```
Variants:
```bash
# conditional scale (only if current matches)
kubectl scale deployment/frontend --current-replicas=2 --replicas=4

# scale everything matching a label
kubectl scale deployment -l app=web --replicas=3

# scale to zero (stop pods, keep the object)
kubectl scale deployment/frontend --replicas=0
```

### Flags
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--replicas=N` | desired count (required) |
| `--current-replicas=N` | precondition: only scale if current == N |
| `--resource-version=V` | precondition: only scale if RV matches (optimistic lock) |
| `-l, --selector` | scale all matching resources |

### Scale vs rollout — what changes
| Operation | Field changed | Pod template changed? | New ReplicaSet? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scale` | `.spec.replicas` | **no** | no — same RS, more/fewer pods |
| `set image` / `set env` / `set resources` | `.spec.template.*` | yes | yes — rolling update |
| `rollout restart` | template annotation | yes (annotation) | yes |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get deploy frontend                 # READY 4/4
kubectl get deploy frontend -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'; echo
kubectl get rs -l app=frontend              # same RS, DESIRED 4
```

### Interaction with HorizontalPodAutoscaler
If an **HPA** targets this Deployment, it continuously writes `.spec.replicas` based on metrics. A manual `kubectl scale` is **reconciled away within one HPA sync** (default ~15s). To hold a manual count you must delete/suspend the HPA, or set its min==max.
```bash
kubectl get hpa
kubectl describe hpa frontend     # shows current/target and last scale actions
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No rollout on scale.** If a question says "without triggering a rollout, change replica count", `scale` is the answer — not editing the template.
- **HPA overrides manual scale.** Always check `kubectl get hpa` before being surprised your count snapped back.
- **Scaling up can leave pods `Pending`** if the cluster can't fit them (resources, taints, affinity) — scale success ≠ all Ready.
- **`--replicas=0` is valid** and does not delete the Deployment; it's a clean pause.
- Don't delete+recreate to change count — loses history/annotations and is the wrong instinct.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend      # READY 4/4
```

questions.title: Rolling image update
questions.teach:
`kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<newimg>` changes the pod template, triggering a **rolling update** (new ReplicaSet scales up while the old scales down). Do it in place; watch with `kubectl rollout status`.

**Gotcha:** the container name isn't always the deployment name — check it first with `kubectl get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}'`.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `api` in `deploy-learn` runs `nginx:1.25` (container named `api`). Perform a rolling update to `nginx:1.26` in place.

Target: the update to `nginx:1.26` is recorded in `api`'s ReplicaSet history (this evidence survives the rollback in the next step).
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api

verification.description: api rolling-updated to nginx:1.26 (recorded in history)

questions.eli5:
Updating the image of a Deployment is like a restaurant switching to a new supplier without ever closing. Instead of shutting the kitchen, the manager brings in a dish made with the new ingredients, serves it, then quietly retires one old dish — over and over — until everything on the menu is the new version. Customers never see an empty counter.

Behind the scenes, when you change the image, Kubernetes creates a **new ReplicaSet** (a fresh batch of pods with `nginx:1.26`) and slowly scales it **up** while scaling the **old** batch (`nginx:1.25`) **down**. That's a **rolling update**.

`kubectl set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26` does exactly this in place. The format is `<container-name>=<new-image>`.

The tricky part: you must name the **container**, and its name isn't always the same as the Deployment's name. Always check first.

**Watch out for:**

- **The container name may differ from the Deployment name.** Check it: `kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}'`. Here they happen to both be `api`, but don't assume.
- **Use `kubectl rollout status` to watch it finish** — the command returns immediately but the roll takes time.
- The **old ReplicaSet isn't deleted** — it's scaled to 0 and kept, which is exactly what makes the next step's rollback possible.
- A typo in the image (a tag that doesn't exist) leaves pods stuck `ImagePullBackOff`; the rollout stalls rather than erroring loudly.
- Only the **image** changed here — the rest of the template stays the same.
questions.deepDive:
## Rolling image update — full rundown

### Mental model
Changing `.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image` is a **template change**, so the Deployment rolls. It creates a **new ReplicaSet** for the new pod-template hash and gradually shifts pods: new RS scales **up**, old RS scales **down**, bounded by `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`. The old RS is retained at 0 replicas (history for rollback).

### The command
```bash
kubectl set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26
#                               └ctr┘ └ new image┘
kubectl rollout status deployment/api     # block until complete
```
`set image` takes **`<containerName>=<image>`** pairs; you can set several:
```bash
kubectl set image deployment/web app=app:v2 sidecar=proxy:v3
kubectl set image deployment/web '*=myrepo/all:v2'   # all containers
```

### Find the container name first
```bash
kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].name}'; echo
```
The container name is **not necessarily** the Deployment name — using the wrong name makes `set image` a no-op (or errors).

### Watch / confirm the rollout
```bash
kubectl rollout status  deployment/api
kubectl rollout history deployment/api            # revision list
kubectl get rs -l app=api -o wide                 # new RS up, old RS at 0
kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'; echo
```

### Rolling-update tuning (for context)
| Field | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `maxSurge` | 25% | extra pods allowed above desired during the roll |
| `maxUnavailable` | 25% | pods allowed unavailable during the roll |
| `minReadySeconds` | 0 | how long a new pod must be Ready before counted available |
| `progressDeadlineSeconds` | 600 | mark rollout `Failed` if no progress in this time |

### Recording the change
Older kubectl had `--record`; it's deprecated. The revision history still tracks the new RS. To annotate a revision with a reason:
```bash
kubectl annotate deployment/api \
  kubernetes.io/change-cause="set image to nginx:1.26"
```
This shows up in `rollout history` under CHANGE-CAUSE.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Wrong container name** → `set image` silently does nothing useful. Verify the name first.
- **`set image` returns immediately**; the actual roll is async — use `rollout status` to confirm.
- **Bad tag → `ImagePullBackOff`** and the rollout **stalls** (respecting `maxUnavailable` it won't take down healthy pods); it eventually fails at `progressDeadlineSeconds`.
- **Old ReplicaSet is kept** (scaled to 0) — this is what enables `rollout undo`. `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) controls how many old RSes are retained.
- Editing only the image leaves the rest of the template intact — but **`rollout undo` reverts the entire template**, not just the image (see rollback lesson).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy api \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}'; echo   # confirm 'api'
kubectl -n deploy-learn set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api
```

questions.title: Roll back a bad release
questions.teach:
`kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` reverts the pod template to the previous revision in place (use `--to-revision=N` for a specific one). List revisions with `kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>`.

**Gotcha:** undo restores the **whole** pod template of that revision (image, env, resources…), not just the image — so roll back *before* layering on other template edits.
questions.prompt:
`nginx:1.26` misbehaves. Roll `api` back so its image returns to `nginx:1.25`.

Target: `api`'s current image is `nginx:1.25` again and the rollout is complete (3/3).
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout undo deployment/api`, then `rollout status`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout undo deployment/api
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api

verification.description: api rolled back to nginx:1.25 (rollout complete)

questions.eli5:
You shipped a new version and it's misbehaving. Good news: Kubernetes keeps the **old versions on the shelf** like saved drafts of a document. Rolling back is just hitting "undo" — restore the previous draft and the app goes back to how it was.

`kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` reverts the Deployment to its **previous** revision. Want a specific older one? `--to-revision=N`. To see the list of saved drafts, `kubectl rollout history deployment/api`.

Under the hood it's the same rolling swap as before — it scales the old (good) ReplicaSet back up and the bad one down — so there's no downtime.

The one thing people trip over: **undo restores the *entire* saved draft, not just the thing you think went wrong.** If the bad revision also had a different env var or resource setting baked in, those come back too — because a "revision" is a snapshot of the whole pod template, not just the image.

**Watch out for:**

- **Undo restores the WHOLE pod template of that revision** — image, env, resources, everything. Not just the image. So roll back *before* you layer new edits on top, or you'll clobber them.
- **`rollout undo` with no flag means "the previous revision"** — one step back. Use `--to-revision=N` to jump to a specific one.
- A **rollback is itself a new rollout** — it takes time; confirm with `kubectl rollout status` and check for 3/3 ready.
- `kubectl rollout history` shows revisions; use `--revision=N` to see one revision's template details.
- You can only roll back to revisions still in history — `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) caps how many are kept.
questions.deepDive:
## Roll back a bad release — full rundown

### Mental model
Every template change creates a **revision**, backed by a retained ReplicaSet. `kubectl rollout undo` switches the Deployment back to a prior revision by scaling that RS up and the current one down — a normal rolling update in reverse. A revision is a **full snapshot of the pod template**, so undo restores *everything* in it, not just the image.

### The commands
```bash
kubectl rollout history deployment/api             # list revisions
kubectl rollout history deployment/api --revision=3  # inspect revision 3's template
kubectl rollout undo    deployment/api             # back to the PREVIOUS revision
kubectl rollout undo    deployment/api --to-revision=2  # to a specific revision
kubectl rollout status  deployment/api             # wait for completion
```

### How revisions/ReplicaSets map
| Revision | ReplicaSet | Template (e.g.) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | api-abc (0 replicas) | nginx:1.25 |
| 2 | api-def (active) | nginx:1.26 |

`undo` from rev 2 → reactivates rev-1's RS (nginx:1.25). Note: undoing **creates a new revision number** that reuses the old template (so history grows; the restored content, not the number, is what reverts).

### What "undo" reverts
Everything in the pod template of the target revision:
- container image(s)
- env / envFrom
- resources (requests/limits)
- command/args, volumes, probes, labels on the template, etc.

So if rev 2 changed both image **and** an env var, undoing to rev 1 reverts **both**. Roll back *before* layering unrelated edits.

### Revision retention
```yaml
spec:
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10   # default; old RSes beyond this are garbage-collected
```
You can only `undo`/`--to-revision` to revisions still retained. Setting it to 0 disables rollback.

### change-cause (history annotation)
```bash
kubectl annotate deployment/api kubernetes.io/change-cause="rollback to 1.25"
kubectl rollout history deployment/api   # CHANGE-CAUSE column
```

### Verify the rollback
```bash
kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'; echo  # nginx:1.25
kubectl rollout status deployment/api     # "successfully rolled out"
kubectl get deploy api                     # READY 3/3
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Undo restores the ENTIRE template**, not just the image — the classic trap. Any other edits in the bad revision come back.
- **Bare `undo` = previous revision only.** For a specific one use `--to-revision=N`; `--to-revision=0` also means "previous".
- **Rollback is a real rollout** — async; confirm with `rollout status` and ready count (here 3/3), don't assume instant.
- **Only retained revisions are reachable** — `revisionHistoryLimit` caps them (default 10).
- `rollout history` shows minimal info unless a `change-cause`/record exists; use `--revision=N` to see template details.
- Rolling back doesn't delete the "bad" RS — it's kept (scaled to 0) and can be rolled forward to again.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout history deployment/api
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout undo    deployment/api        # or --to-revision=N
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status  deployment/api        # 3/3, image back to nginx:1.25
```
